youtube.title: Standard Oil: How Rockefeller Controlled 90% of US Oil and Got Richer
youtube.description:
Standard Oil was the company that made John D. Rockefeller the richest man of his age, refining roughly nine of every ten barrels of oil in America by about 1880. This documentary shows how Rockefeller got rich by buying refineries instead of drilling, from the 1865 auction to the 1872 Cleveland deals. Then came the Standard Oil breakup in 1911: how did splitting the company into 34 pieces make him even richer?

This documentary follows the decision that built Standard Oil: the 1865 auction where Rockefeller bid $72,500 against his own partner, the railroad deals, the six weeks in 1872 when he bought most of Cleveland's refineries, the backlash from Ida Tarbell and the Sherman Act, and the 1911 Supreme Court break-up into 34 companies that still run today as Exxon Mobil, Chevron and part of BP.

sources.claim: By about 1880 Standard Oil controlled about 90 percent of US oil refining
sources.source: Ron Chernow, Titan: The Life of John D. Rockefeller, Sr. (Random House, 1998); Daniel Yergin, The Prize (Simon & Schuster, 1991)

sources.claim: Rockefeller and his partner Maurice Clark disagreed over how much he borrowed to expand the refinery
sources.source: Chernow, Titan (1998), ch. 5

sources.claim: In February 1865 the partners auctioned the refinery between themselves; Clark bid $72,000 and Rockefeller won at $72,500
sources.source: Chernow, Titan (1998), ch. 5

sources.claim: Rockefeller later called the auction 'the day that determined my career'
sources.source: Rockefeller's recollections, quoted in Chernow, Titan (1998), ch. 5

sources.claim: John D. Rockefeller was born on 8 July 1839, so he was twenty-five at the February 1865 auction
sources.source: Chernow, Titan (1998), ch. 1

sources.claim: Exxon Mobil and Chevron together reported more than $500 billion in total revenues in 2024
sources.source: Exxon Mobil Corp. Form 10-K for 2024 (filed Feb 2025); Chevron Corp. Form 10-K for 2024 (filed Feb 2025)

sources.claim: On 15 May 1911 the US Supreme Court upheld the dissolution of Standard Oil, which was split into 34 companies
sources.source: Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey v. United States, 221 U.S. 1 (1911); Chernow, Titan (1998)

sources.claim: Before electric light, American homes were lit after dark by kerosene, the main product of refining
sources.source: Yergin, The Prize (1991), ch. 1-2

sources.claim: Kerosene became one of America's leading exports, shipped to Europe and Asia
sources.source: Yergin, The Prize (1991), ch. 3

sources.claim: Edwin Drake's well near Titusville, Pennsylvania struck oil in August 1859 at about 69 feet, and a rush to drill followed
sources.source: Yergin, The Prize (1991), ch. 1; Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission, Drake Well Museum

sources.claim: Drillers poured into the Oil Creek valley after Drake's strike, taking leases to drill
sources.source: Yergin, The Prize (1991), ch. 1

sources.claim: Crude sold for about $10 a barrel in January 1861 and as little as 10 cents by the end of that year
sources.source: Yergin, The Prize (1991), ch. 1

sources.claim: Pithole, Pennsylvania grew from farmland to roughly 15,000 people in 1865 and was largely abandoned within about two years
sources.source: Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission, Pithole City site; Yergin, The Prize (1991), ch. 1

sources.claim: Cleveland lies more than a hundred miles west of the Oil Creek region
sources.source: Great-circle distance between Cleveland, Ohio (41.50N, 81.69W) and Titusville, Pennsylvania (41.63N, 79.67W), about 105 miles; coordinates from the USGS Geographic Names Information System

sources.claim: In 1863 Rockefeller and Clark backed a Cleveland refinery run by Samuel Andrews
sources.source: Chernow, Titan (1998), ch. 5

sources.claim: Refining heated crude in iron stills to draw off kerosene; a small refinery was cheap to build and Cleveland had dozens
sources.source: Chernow, Titan (1998), ch. 5-6; Yergin, The Prize (1991), ch. 2

sources.claim: After the auction Rockefeller owned the largest refinery in Cleveland
sources.source: Chernow, Titan (1998), ch. 5

sources.claim: Henry Flagler joined the firm in 1867
sources.source: Chernow, Titan (1998), ch. 6

sources.claim: In 1868 Flagler secured a Lake Shore Railroad rate of $1.65 a barrel to New York against a posted $2.40, in return for a steady 60 carloads a day
sources.source: Chernow, Titan (1998), ch. 6

sources.claim: Standard Oil Company (Ohio) was incorporated on 10 January 1870 with $1 million in capital
sources.source: Chernow, Titan (1998), ch. 7

sources.claim: In 1870 Standard Oil refined about one-tenth of America's oil
sources.source: Chernow, Titan (1998), ch. 7

sources.claim: 'The day of combination is here to stay. Individualism has gone, never to return.'
sources.source: Rockefeller, interviews with William O. Inglis (c. 1917-1920), quoted in Chernow, Titan (1998)

sources.claim: In about six weeks in early 1872 Standard Oil bought 22 of Cleveland's 26 refineries, often paying in Standard shares
sources.source: Chernow, Titan (1998), ch. 8; Ida Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company (1904)

sources.claim: Some sellers later said they felt they had no choice
sources.source: Testimony and accounts collected in Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company (1904)

sources.claim: The South Improvement Company promised member refiners rebates and payments on rivals' shipments; when it became known, producers held mass protests in February 1872
sources.source: Chernow, Titan (1998), ch. 8; Tarbell (1904), ch. 2-3

sources.claim: Pennsylvania repealed the South Improvement Company's charter in April 1872; it never went into operation
sources.source: Chernow, Titan (1998), ch. 8

sources.claim: Through the 1870s Standard joined refiners in Pittsburgh, Philadelphia and New York, often through secret alliances
sources.source: Chernow, Titan (1998), ch. 9-10

sources.claim: Kerosene fell from about 58 cents a gallon in 1865 to 26 cents in 1870 and about 8 cents in 1885
sources.source: Chernow, Titan (1998)

sources.claim: Independent producers opened the Tidewater pipeline in 1879, over 100 miles long; Standard built its own lines and later bought into Tidewater
sources.source: Yergin, The Prize (1991), ch. 2; Chernow, Titan (1998), ch. 11

sources.claim: The Standard Oil Trust was formed in 1882 under nine trustees
sources.source: Chernow, Titan (1998), ch. 12

sources.claim: Congress passed the Sherman Antitrust Act in 1890
sources.source: Sherman Antitrust Act, 26 Stat. 209 (2 July 1890)

sources.claim: Ohio's Supreme Court ordered the trust dissolved in 1892; by 1899 the companies sat under Standard Oil of New Jersey
sources.source: State ex rel. Watson v. Standard Oil Co., 49 Ohio St. 137 (1892); Chernow, Titan (1998)

sources.claim: Ida Tarbell's father was an independent oil producer in Pennsylvania
sources.source: Ida Tarbell, All in the Day's Work (1939); Chernow, Titan (1998)

sources.claim: Tarbell's series on Standard Oil ran in McClure's from November 1902 and was collected as a book in 1904
sources.source: McClure's Magazine, Nov 1902 onward; Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company (McClure, Phillips, 1904)

sources.claim: Tarbell's articles turned public opinion against Standard Oil
sources.source: Chernow, Titan (1998), on the reception of Tarbell's McClure's series

sources.claim: 'Mr. Rockefeller has systematically played with loaded dice'
sources.source: Ida Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company (1904)

sources.claim: The federal government sued Standard Oil under the Sherman Act in November 1906
sources.source: United States v. Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey, filed Nov 1906, US Circuit Court, Eastern District of Missouri

sources.claim: In 1909 the federal circuit court ruled against Standard Oil
sources.source: United States v. Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey, 173 F. 177 (C.C.E.D. Mo. 1909)

sources.claim: After Spindletop in 1901, rivals such as Gulf and Texaco grew outside Standard's control; its refining share fell to about 64 percent by 1911
sources.source: Yergin, The Prize (1991), ch. 4-5

sources.claim: The court gave Standard six months to dissolve
sources.source: Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey v. United States, 221 U.S. 1 (1911)

sources.claim: By one account Rockefeller heard the ruling on a golf course and told a companion to buy Standard Oil
sources.source: Chernow, Titan (1998), ch. 29

sources.claim: Rockefeller held about a quarter of the shares of each successor company, and their shares rose after the break-up
sources.source: Chernow, Titan (1998), ch. 29

sources.claim: Rockefeller's fortune was estimated at about $900 million in 1913
sources.source: Chernow, Titan (1998)

sources.claim: Jersey Standard became Exxon and Standard of New York became Mobil; they merged in 1999
sources.source: Exxon Mobil Corp. corporate history; Exxon-Mobil merger completed 30 Nov 1999 (FTC consent order, 1999)

sources.claim: Standard of California became Chevron; Standard of Indiana became Amoco, merged with BP in 1998; Standard Oil of Ohio, known as Sohio, was fully taken over by BP in 1987
sources.source: Chevron Corp. corporate history; BP plc corporate history (Standard Oil Company of Ohio, 'Sohio', BP majority from 1978, full acquisition 1987)

sources.claim: Standard moved seriously into crude production in the late 1880s with Ohio's Lima field, Rockefeller offering to risk his own money when colleagues doubted it
sources.source: Chernow, Titan (1998), ch. 15; John D. Rockefeller, Random Reminiscences of Men and Events (1909)
